name: Rumi
info: Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Balkhī, known as Rumi, was a thirteenth-century Persian-language Sufi mystic and poet who lived in Konya in Anatolia; he is remembered for the Masnavi and as the figure from whom the Mevlevi Order descends.

facts.born: 30 September 1207, to Persian parents at Wakhsh, a village in present-day Tajikistan; son of the preacher and jurist Bahā ud-Dīn Walad, of a family of Hanafi preachers, and Mu'mina Khātūn
facts.died: 17 December 1273, at Konya in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm, after falling ill that month; buried beside his father
facts.role: Head of his father's madrassa in Konya from the age of twenty-five; Islamic jurist, preacher and teacher; Sufi master and poet
facts.known: The Masnavi, a six-volume poem of about 27,000 lines; the Divan of Shams-e Tabrizi; his bond with the dervish Shams-e Tabrizi; teaching music, poetry and dance as a path to God; the Mevlevi Order of the Whirling Dervishes; the prose Fihi Ma Fihi

t: Rumi was trained as an Islamic scholar and succeeded his father as head of a madrassa in Konya, where his family had settled after fleeing west before the Mongols.
His meeting with the wandering dervish Shams-e Tabrizi in 1244, and Shams's disappearance in 1248, turned the jurist into an ascetic and a poet.
He wrote in Persian the Divan and the six books of the Masnavi, and after his death his followers and his son Sultan Walad founded the Mevlevi Order.
dyk: Rumi wrote in Persian, his mother tongue, but his Divan also holds 90 ghazals and 19 quatrains in Arabic, a couple of dozen or so couplets in Turkish and 14 couplets in Greek, the Greek all in three poems that mix Greek and Persian.
ev: Rumi is born at Wakhsh, where his father, Bahā ud-Dīn Walad, is a preacher and jurist
The family moves to Samarkand when he is aged around five
He marries Gowhar Khatun at Karaman, where the family has settled on its way west
His father settles the family at Konya in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm
He meets the dervish Shams-e Tabrizi, a meeting that changes him from a teacher and jurist into an ascetic
Shams is called to the back door one night and is never seen again
He dies at Konya and is buried beside his father; his followers found the Mevlevi Order

sections.early:
Rumi was born on 30 September 1207 to Persian parents at Wakhsh, a village in present-day Tajikistan. His father, Bahā ud-Dīn Walad, was a theologian, jurist and mystic who preached there and whom Rumi's followers later called Sultan al-Ulama, "Sultan of the Scholars"; his mother was Mu'mina Khātūn. For several generations the family had been preachers of the relatively liberal Hanafi Maturidi school. Later accounts made Rumi a descendant of Abu Bakr and, through his mother's line, of the Khwarazmshah; some modern scholars reject the first claim, and the second is seen as a hagiographical tradition meant to link the family with royalty.

The area was culturally adjacent to Balkh, then a major centre of Persian culture where Sufism had developed for several centuries. Besides his father, who was connected to the spiritual lineage of Najm al-Din Kubra, the strongest influences on Rumi were the Persian poets Attar and Sanai. The family lived at Wakhsh until 1212, when Rumi was about five, and then moved to Samarkand.

When the Mongols invaded Central Asia, sometime between 1215 and 1220, Bahā ud-Dīn set out westwards with his whole family and a group of disciples. A hagiographical account, not accepted by all Rumi scholars, has the poet Attar meet them at Nishapur and say of father and son, "Here comes a sea followed by an ocean." The caravan went on to Baghdad, made the pilgrimage to Mecca, and passed through Damascus and several Anatolian towns before settling for seven years at Karaman, where Rumi's mother and brother died.
sections.rise:
At Karaman in 1225 Rumi married Gowhar Khatun, with whom he had two sons, Sultan Walad and Ala-eddin Chalabi; after her death he married again and had another son and a daughter. On 1 May 1228, most likely on the insistent invitation of 'Alā' ud-Dīn Key-Qobād, ruler of Anatolia, his father settled at Konya, in the westernmost territories of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm. Anatolia had until recently belonged to the Eastern Roman Empire and was still known to Arabs, Persians and Turks as Rum, which is the source of the name Rumi.

Bahā ud-Dīn became head of a madrassa, and when he died Rumi, aged twenty-five, inherited his position. One of his father's students, Sayyed Burhan ud-Din Muhaqqiq Termazi, went on training him in the Shariah and in the Sufi path, and for nine years Rumi practised Sufism as his disciple, until Burhan ud-Din died in 1240 or 1241. His public life then began: he became an Islamic jurist, issued fatwas, gave sermons in the mosques of Konya and taught in the madrassa. In this period he also travelled to Damascus and is said to have spent four years there.

On 15 November 1244 he met the wandering dervish Shams-e Tabrizi, and the meeting changed his life: from an accomplished teacher and jurist he became an ascetic. Shams, the story goes, had travelled the Middle East praying for someone who could "endure my company", and a voice had named Jalal ud-Din of Konya. Sufi mysticism places great emphasis on the bond of master and disciple. Rumi and Shams became so absorbed in each other that Rumi neglected his duties.
sections.deeds:
Rumi's poetry began with the loss of Shams in 1248. His love and his bereavement found expression in an outpouring of lyric poems, gathered as the Dīwān-e Kabīr or Dīwān-e Shams-e Tabrīzī, named in honour of his master. It holds approximately 35,000 Persian couplets and 2,000 Persian quatrains. His best-known work is the Masnavi, a poem in six books of approximately 27,000 lines that weaves fables, scenes from everyday life, Qur'anic revelation and exegesis, and metaphysics together. He dictated it over twelve years to his scribe and favourite student, Hussam-e Chalabi, who had suggested a book in the manner of Sanai and Attar; it opens, "Listen to the reed and the tale it tells, how it sings of separation". It has commonly been called "the Quran in Persian".

His prose survives in three collections. Fihi Ma Fihi records seventy-one talks and lectures, compiled from his disciples' notes; the Majāles-e Sab'a holds seven sermons on the deeper meaning of Qur'an and Hadith; and the Makatib gathers his letters to disciples, family members and men of state.

Like other Sufi poets of Persian literature, he speaks of a love that infuses the world. In his terms tawhid, the oneness of God, is lived most fully through love, which he calls "that flame which, when it blazes up, burns away everything except the Everlasting Beloved". He believed passionately in music, poetry and dance as a path for reaching God, and encouraged sama, listening to music and turning in the sacred dance; from these ideas the whirling of the dervishes developed into a ritual.
sections.opponents:
The gravest controversy of Rumi's life concerns Shams. On the night of 5 December 1248, as the two were talking, Shams was called to the back door, went out and was never seen again. There are many theories about his disappearance; the most popular are that Rumi's youngest son killed him, that he was killed for blasphemy, or that Shams, a known wanderer, simply chose to move on. For more than a month Rumi refused to believe the rumours of his death; after forty days he accepted it and began to dress in black.

The record of his life is itself disputed. The main biography, the Manāqib ul-Ārifīn of Shams ud-Din Ahmad Aflāki, written between 1318 and 1353, is hagiographical and mixes legend with fact; Franklin Lewis, author of the most complete modern biography, treats the hagiographical and the actual life in separate sections.

His religious outlook has been read in different ways. His work carries traces of religious pluralism, as in the line "the lamps are different, but the Light is the same", yet he clearly holds the superiority of Islam, calls Muhammad the most perfect of the prophets and criticises Christianity for "overloading the image of God with superfluous structures and complications". Shibli Nomani argued that he should be seen as a serious theologian and not solely as a mystical poet. Edward G. Browne noted that Rumi, Sanai and Attar were all Sunni Muslims; according to Annemarie Schimmel, the tendency of Shia authors to count Rumi among their own grew stronger after Twelver Shia became the state religion of the Safavid Empire in 1501.
sections.last:
After Shams, Rumi found another companion in Salaḥ ud-Din-e Zarkub, a goldsmith, who served him for a decade. Zarkub was illiterate and pronounced some words incorrectly, and Rumi used some of those words in his poems as a sign of support and humility towards him. Rumi named him his successor, but Zarkub died first. Hussam-e Chalabi, his scribe, then took the companion's place. Walking with him one day in the Meram vineyards outside Konya, Hussam proposed that Rumi write a long poem; Rumi is said to have taken out a paper bearing the opening eighteen lines of the Masnavi, and the dictation of its six volumes filled the next twelve years.

In December 1273 Rumi fell ill. He predicted his own death and composed a ghazal that begins, "How doest thou know what sort of king I have within me as companion?" He died at Konya on 17 December 1273. The diverse community of the city mourned him, and local Christians and Jews joined the crowd as his body was carried through the streets. He was buried beside his father, and a shrine, the "Green Tomb", whose building his close friend the Georgian princess and Seljuq queen Tamar Gurju Khatun sponsored, was raised over the grave.

His followers founded the Mevlevi Order after his death. Its first head was Hussam Chalabi; when he died in 1284, Rumi's only surviving son, Sultan Walad, who died in 1312, was installed as grand master, and it was he who organised the order. Its leadership has remained in Rumi's family at Konya without interruption since.
sections.legacy:
The Mevlevi, known as the Whirling Dervishes, perform their dhikr as sama, to music set to poems from the Masnavi and the Divan. The order was well established in the Ottoman Empire. On 13 December 1925 the Republic of Turkey under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk passed a law closing all dervish lodges, dissolving the Sufi orders and banning their ceremonies. In 1927 Rumi's mausoleum at Konya was allowed to reopen as a museum, and in the 1950s the government began to let the dervishes perform once a year in Konya. In 2005 UNESCO proclaimed the Mevlevi Sama Ceremony a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

Many Muslims, particularly in the Turko-Persian cultural sphere, regard the Masnavi as one of the most important works of Islamic literature, and many commentators have called it the greatest mystical poem in world literature. Rumi's poetry influenced Persian literature and the literary traditions of Ottoman Turkish, Chagatai, Pashto, Kurdish, Urdu and Bengali. In Iran his verse is displayed on city walls, sung in Persian music and read in school books, and it forms the basis of much classical Iranian and Afghan music.

His shrine remains a place of pilgrimage. His works have been translated into many languages; the English interpretations by Coleman Barks have sold more than half a million copies, and he has been described as the best-selling poet in the United States. UNESCO was associated in 2007 with the eight-hundredth anniversary of his birth, which Turkey marked with a televised sama.

summary: Rumi, born in 1207 in what is now Tajikistan, settled with his family at Konya in Anatolia and became a jurist and preacher. His bond with the dervish Shams-e Tabrizi made him a poet; he wrote the Divan and the Masnavi in Persian. After his death in 1273 his followers founded the Mevlevi Order.
references: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West (Oneworld Publications, 2000)
Annemarie Schimmel, The Triumphal Sun: A Study of the Works of Jalaloddin Rumi (SUNY Press, 1993)
Fatemeh Keshavarz, Reading Mystical Lyric: The Case of Jalal al-Din Rumi (University of South Carolina Press, 1998)
William Chittick, The Sufi Doctrine of Rumi (World Wisdom, 2005)
Afzal Iqbal, The Life and thought of Mohammad Jalal-ud-Din Rumi (Bazm-i-Iqbal, 1959)
notes: Birthplace: the article's body says Wakhsh in present-day Tajikistan; the lead calls him 'Balkhī' and says the family 'hailed from Balkh'. I followed the body.

The 'opponents' section: the article names no opponents or critics of Rumi in his lifetime. I filled it with the Shams controversy, the reliability of the hagiography, and the disputes over his religious outlook and denomination, all as the article gives them. It is the weakest fit to the guide's heading.

Ages do not agree in the article: the lead says he settled in Konya 'at age 19' but the body dates the settlement 1 May 1228 (he would be 20); the Attar meeting is said to have impressed 'the eighteen-year-old Rumi' though the flight is dated 1215-1220 (he would be 8-13). I gave neither age. The article also has him marry in Karaman in 1225 during a seven-year stay that ends with the 1228 move.

Father's death: no year in the article, only that Rumi was twenty-five. The order of events (nine years with Burhan ud-Din to 1240/1241, four years in Damascus 'during this period') is as the article gives it.

The article says the meeting with Shams was on 15 November 1244 and the disappearance on 5 December 1248; 'infatuated with each other, causing Rumi to neglect his duties' is the lead's wording, which I softened to 'so absorbed in each other'.
'Rumi's youngest son killed him' is given as one of the 'most popular' theories, unattributed in the article.
Aflaki: the article says his Manāqib was 'written between 1318 and 1353' and elsewhere dates 'Shamsuddin Aflaki (c.1286 to 1291)', which is unclear; I used only the first.

Mevlevi Order: the article says both that 'his followers and his son Sultan Walad founded' it upon his death, that it 'was founded in 1273 by Rumi's followers', and that Sultan Walad 'organised' it. Sultan Walad is called 'Rumi's younger and only surviving son' though listed first of the sons; I wrote 'only surviving son'.

Masnavi length: 'approximately 27,000 lines'; Divan 'approximately 35000 Persian couplets and 2000 Persian quatrains'. 'Best selling poet' in the US is the lead's claim, softened to 'has been described as'.
The tomb: 'a shrine ... whose building Gurju Khatun sponsored' joins two statements of the article (the Green Tomb; 'She was the one who sponsored the construction of his tomb').

Wanted but not in the article: the year of his father's death; when the Masnavi was begun and finished; Salah ud-Din's death year; who opposed Shams in Konya and Shams's first departure; the name of his second wife; any contemporary criticism of sama.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
